options.B: Unrinsed shampoo actively accelerates hair follicle growth
options.C: Remaining soap prevents the hair from absorbing water
options.D: Residue permanently changes the natural color of the hair

explanation: Leaving soap behind can dry out the skin and make the scalp itchy and flaky. A good rinse keeps your patient comfortable! [learn more](GNS112_U5_T5#GNS112_U5_T5_h3)

question: What is the most immediate life-threatening complication of untreated, profuse watery diarrhea?

options.A: Hypovolemic shock from fluid loss
options.B: Enlargement of the liver and spleen
options.C: Permanent blockage of the colon
options.D: High blood pressure and stroke

explanation: Losing massive amounts of body fluid without adequate replacement drops blood volume dangerously low, leading to shock and organ failure. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T20#GNS313_U2_T20_h6)

question: Which finding around a skeletal traction pin site should you report as a sign of infection?

options.A: Purulent drainage and foul odor
options.B: Dry crusting around the metal insertion point
options.C: Mild pinkness that fades within the first day
options.D: Small amounts of clear serosanguinous drainage

explanation: You got it! Pus and bad smells are telltale signs of bacteria at work. Light pinkness or dry crusting can just be normal early healing.

question: What key detail does a drug label tell you about its strength?

options.A: The amount of active drug per tablet, capsule, or milliliter
options.B: The name of the drug rep
options.C: The patient's diagnosis
options.D: How much the hospital paid for it

explanation: The label strength tells you the concentration—how much medicine is actually packed into each pill or mL.

question: Why is proper lighting and full exposure of the joint necessary during a musculoskeletal assessment?

options.A: To make it easier for the doctor to read the laboratory results
options.B: To prevent the patient from feeling cold in the examination room
options.C: To ensure the patient's blood pressure remains stable throughout the test
options.D: To accurately observe subtle skin changes, swelling, and muscle symmetry

explanation: Good light and clear visibility let the nurse spot minor differences in size, shape, or color between limbs. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T3#GNS222_U1_T3_h2)

question: What is the term for a piece of dead bone separated from living bone during osteomyelitis?

options.A: Cortex
options.B: Involucrum
options.C: Callus
options.D: Sequestrum

explanation: A sequestrum is the segment of necrotic bone that has lost its blood supply due to severe infection and pressure. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h3)

question: What is the main purpose of the cheeks and lips during the process of eating?

options.A: They keep food positioned between the teeth for effective chewing.
options.B: They absorb water from the food bolus before it reaches the stomach.
options.C: They filter out harmful bacteria found naturally on raw foods.
options.D: They secrete digestive enzymes that immediately dissolve tough fibers.

explanation: The muscular walls of the lips and cheeks press inward to keep food in the correct spot while the teeth grind it down. [learn more](GNS121_U1_T1#GNS121_U1_T1_h2)

question: Which drug class is most risky for a fatal overdose because it lacks a simple reversal drug?

options.A: Z-drugs
options.B: Barbiturates
options.C: Antihistamines
options.D: Benzodiazepines

explanation: Barbiturates are very strong. Unlike benzodiazepines which have a handy reversal drug like flumazenil, barbiturates can easily cause fatal breathing arrest. [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h2)

question: Why do doctors frequently prescribe corticosteroid medications to patients with brain tumors?

options.A: To reduce brain swelling and intracranial pressure
options.B: To cure the underlying cancer cells completely
options.C: To lower the patient's blood pressure levels
options.D: To prevent the patient from developing an infection

explanation: Well done! Steroids like dexamethasone are lifesavers here. They don't kill the cancer, but they quickly shrink the puffy swelling (edema) around the tumor, bringing relief fast.

question: An employer demands to see the full medical diagnosis and lab results of a worker who visited your clinic. What are you ethically allowed to share?

options.A: The complete confidential medical history and psychiatric notes
options.B: Only the worker's fitness-for-work status and necessary job accommodations
options.C: No information whatsoever, ever
options.D: Detailed lab test values and family health records

explanation: You nailed it! To keep trust and protect privacy, you only tell the boss if the worker is fit for duty or needs special adjustments—keep the private diagnosis to yourself.

question: How do proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) help treat peptic ulcers?

options.A: By blocking the enzyme system responsible for acid secretion
options.B: By killing all bacteria residing in the digestive tract
options.C: By neutralizing stomach acid the moment it enters the gut
options.D: By coating the entire stomach lining with a sticky barrier

explanation: Correct! PPIs turn off the tiny acid pumps in the stomach lining, drastically cutting down the amount of acid produced so the ulcer can heal.

question: What type of medication is given to the scalp right before placing traction pins?

options.A: Topical antibiotic cream
options.B: Intravenous general anesthetic
options.C: Oral muscle relaxant
options.D: Local anesthetic

explanation: A local anesthetic is injected right where the pins will go so the patient stays completely numb and comfortable.

question: What is a common argument progressive religious leaders use to discourage FGM?

options.A: Science proves that cutting actually reduces female fertility
options.B: Federal tax laws require religious houses to condemn the act
options.C: The practice is just a cultural tradition, not a divine religious requirement
options.D: International groups will shut down churches and mosques that allow it

explanation: Well done! Clerics often succeed by separating true religious teachings from harmful cultural customs that have no basis in sacred texts.

question: How soon can a patient start ovulating again after an abortion?

options.A: Only after three normal monthly cycles
options.B: After exactly six months
options.C: As early as 10 to 14 days
options.D: Once the patient reaches menopause

explanation: The ovaries can release an egg just two weeks post-abortion, even before bleeding stops. Good to keep in mind for patient education!

question: When is the exact right time to chart a medication you just gave?

options.A: At the end of the entire nursing shift
options.B: Whenever the prescribing doctor asks for updates
options.C: Before preparing the drug at the medication cart
options.D: Immediately after the patient swallows the drug

explanation: Always chart right away after giving it! This stops another nurse from accidentally giving a double dose.

question: Which of these protects an older adult's mental health?

options.A: Living in total isolation from neighbors and family
options.B: Experiencing frequent discrimination and ageism
options.C: Complete financial instability and job insecurity
options.D: A reliable caregiver network and community connections

explanation: A strong circle of family and friends acts like a shield against life stress. Beautiful concept to carry into practice!

question: Which of these is NOT a benefit of regular student evaluation?

options.A: Clearing away all hospital errors forever
options.B: Encouraging steady study habits
options.C: Building your confidence in clinical skills
options.D: Helping you reflect on your own progress

explanation: Evaluations make us much safer, but let's be real—no test can completely wipe out human error in a busy hospital. We're all human!

question: You notice continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber of a chest tube system. What does this usually mean?

options.A: An expected amount of residual blood loss
options.B: An air leak somewhere in the tubing or insertion site
options.C: Blockage of the chest tube drainage lumen
options.D: Normal lung re-expansion and healing

explanation: While tiny occasional bubbles can be normal, continuous bubbling is like a leaky bicycle tire telling us air is getting in where it shouldn't. Excellent clinical observation!

question: Why should nurses avoid cliché phrases like 'time heals all wounds' when talking to someone who is grieving?

options.A: It is scientifically incorrect according to modern psychology
options.B: It can minimize their pain and make them feel dismissed
options.C: It causes immediate physical regression into the denial stage
options.D: It violates standard nursing documentation guidelines

explanation: Spot on! Clichés can shut down honest communication because they make the person feel like their unique pain is being brushed aside.

question: Why do nurses take baseline neurological data when a patient is first admitted?

options.A: To compare with later findings to detect clinical changes
options.B: To calculate the patient's exact hospital discharge date
options.C: To determine the exact cause of a brain tumor
options.D: To replace the need for physician daily rounds

explanation: Having a clear starting point helps you quickly spot any tiny changes if the patient's condition starts to slip later!

question: Which chemical exposure patient needs to be rushed straight to the resuscitation bay?

options.A: A patient with normal vital signs and no symptoms
options.B: A patient with abnormal vital signs and respiratory distress
options.C: A calm patient who smelled fumes outside a factory
options.D: A patient with a mild skin redness on one hand

explanation: If vital signs are crashing and the patient is struggling to breathe, they need immediate, high-priority emergency care.

question: Which technology helps link patient prescriptions directly with pharmacy dispensing software?

options.A: Manual paper ledgers stored in wooden cabinets
options.B: Electronic health records and barcoding systems
options.C: Standard telephone landlines on the ward
options.D: Traditional wall clocks placed in the hallway

explanation: Digital records and barcode scanners speed up order transmission and reduce transcription mistakes between departments. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T4#GNS215_U1_T4_h8)

question: What does 'asepsis' mean in your daily nursing practice?

options.A: The complete destruction of all life forms on human skin
options.B: The chemical disinfection of hospital floors and walls
options.C: The total absence of disease-producing microorganisms
options.D: The administration of prophylactic antibiotics before surgery

explanation: Great job! Asepsis simply means keeping an environment or item free from harmful germs that cause infections. You've got this!

question: A client comes back to the clinic three weeks after getting an IUD with severe lower belly pain, fever, and strange vaginal discharge. What should you suspect first?

options.A: The IUD completely falling out on its own
options.B: Simple iron deficiency anemia
options.C: A normal adjustment period to the device
options.D: Pelvic inflammatory disease

explanation: Fever, foul discharge, and severe lower abdominal pain are classic red flags for an ascending uterine infection like PID. Act fast and evaluate her!

question: A nurse is caring for a bedridden patient with advanced Parkinson's disease. What is the best way to prevent bedsores (skin breakdown)?

options.A: Repositioning the patient every two hours
options.B: Keeping the room temperature very high
options.C: Encouraging the patient to run on a treadmill
options.D: Applying lotion once a week

explanation: Turning or repositioning the patient every two hours takes pressure off bony areas, keeping the skin safe and healthy. Excellent bedside care knowledge!

question: Why must nurses emphasize treating sexual partners when a teenager is diagnosed with a bacterial STI?

options.A: To prevent reinfection of the original patient and control community spread
options.B: To ensure the laboratory technicians have enough test samples
options.C: To fulfill mandatory legal requirements for school attendance
options.D: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing antibiotics

explanation: Spot on! Treating partners stops the 'ping-pong' effect where partners pass the infection right back to each other.

question: Why is oxytocin given right after a baby is delivered?

options.A: To stimulate early breastmilk letdown
options.B: To lower the mother's blood pressure
options.C: To speed up the dilation of the cervix
options.D: To prevent postpartum hemorrhage

explanation: Spot on! Oxytocin makes the uterus clamp down firmly, sealing off blood vessels and keeping heavy bleeding at bay.

question: Which of these is a classic sign that a patient with diarrhoea is starting to get dehydrated?

options.A: Swelling in both lower legs and ankles
options.B: Dry mucous membranes and poor skin turgor
options.C: Excessive production of clear saliva
options.D: Increased blood pressure and flushed skin

explanation: When body fluid drops, tissues lose their bounce and moisture. Look out for a sticky dry mouth and skin that takes a moment to snap back when pinched!

question: Which electrolyte level drops rapidly when a patient suffers from severe, ongoing diarrhea?

options.A: Hypercalcemia
options.B: Hypokalemia
options.C: Hypoglycemia
options.D: Hypernatremia

explanation: Well done! Lower GI fluids are packed with potassium. When diarrhea flushes them out quickly, the patient loses too much potassium, leading to hypokalemia. Every question makes you sharper!

question: Which surgical procedure removes the cyst while keeping the ovary safe and intact?

options.A: Salpingectomy
options.B: Oophorectomy
options.C: Cystectomy
options.D: Hysterectomy

explanation: Notice the suffix '-ectomy' means removal, and 'cyst-' means the cyst itself. A cystectomy takes out just the cyst while saving the ovary and protecting future fertility!

question: How does the World Health Organization (WHO) officially define health?

options.A: The total absence of any infection or physical pain
options.B: The ability to work and function normally in society
options.C: A balance between spiritual and biological body forces
options.D: A state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being

explanation: You've got this! The WHO looks at the whole person. Health isn't just about a strong body; it includes how we feel mentally and how we relate to others around us.

question: What do endocrine glands release straight into the bloodstream?

options.A: Hormones
options.B: Mucus
options.C: Saliva
options.D: Enzymes

explanation: Spot on! Endocrine glands don't use ducts; they release hormones straight into our blood to act as chemical messengers all over the body.

question: Why is secondary prevention so crucial for conditions like type 2 diabetes?

options.A: The disease often develops silently without early symptoms
options.B: Symptoms are always too painful to ignore
options.C: Early detection makes the condition completely disappear
options.D: Screening tests are expensive and rarely performed

explanation: Exactly! Type 2 diabetes can creep up quietly for years without symptoms, making routine screening an absolute lifesaver.

question: What is a major hazard of using physical restraints on an older adult?

options.A: Immediate strengthening of lower limb bone density and balance
options.B: Increased risk of muscle weakness, agitation, and severe injury
options.C: Complete prevention of accidental falls in all clinical settings
options.D: Permanent restoration of full cognitive function and memory

explanation: Restraints do not prevent falls safely; instead, they lead to rapid muscle wasting, emotional distress, and worse injuries when patients try to get free. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T8#GNS225_U5_T8_h5)

question: A village has had 500 total cases of diabetes for ten years, but only 5 people were newly diagnosed this year. What does this mean?

options.A: Both high prevalence and high incidence
options.B: Both low prevalence and low incidence
options.C: High prevalence and low incidence
options.D: Low prevalence and high incidence

explanation: You're getting the hang of it! A large total of ongoing cases means high prevalence, while just a few fresh diagnoses means low incidence.

question: A pregnant patient asks how to manage morning sickness before she even gets out of bed. What is the best tip?

options.A: Brush your teeth thoroughly with strong mint toothpaste first
options.B: Drink a large glass of cold milk immediately upon waking
options.C: Exercise vigorously for ten minutes to boost morning energy
options.D: Keep dry crackers by the bed and eat a few before standing up

explanation: Munching a dry cracker before sitting up lifts blood sugar just enough to calm the stomach before gravity and movement trigger nausea.

question: Which type of ovarian cancer is the most common, making up about 90% of all cases?

options.A: Germ cell tumors
options.B: Stromal cell tumors
options.C: Endodermal sinus tumors
options.D: Epithelial ovarian cancer

explanation: Spot on! Epithelial tumors start from the outer surface lining of the ovary and make up the vast majority of cases we see in practice.

question: Which nursing action best demonstrates tertiary cancer prevention?

options.A: Encouraging a young adult to stop smoking cigarettes before any disease develops
options.B: Teaching arm exercises to a patient recovering from breast cancer surgery to prevent lymphedema
options.C: Providing educational pamphlets about the importance of getting a regular Pap smear
options.D: Administering a routine hepatitis B immunization to a healthcare worker

explanation: Managing complications and rehabilitating a patient post-treatment are core goals of tertiary prevention. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T12#GNS321_U1_T12_h4)

question: What is another common name for a joint in the human body where bones meet?

options.A: Articulation
options.B: Tendon
options.C: Ligament
options.D: Cartilage

explanation: Great start! An 'articulation' is simply the anatomical term for any place where two or more bones meet. You've got this!

question: Why might someone know a health practice is dangerous yet continue doing it?

options.A: They enjoy being sick and visiting the primary health clinic
options.B: Nurses failed to write down the instructions on a chalkboard
options.C: Government laws forbid them from changing their personal habits
options.D: Economic, social, or cultural barriers make the healthy choice difficult

explanation: So true! Knowing what to do is only half the battle. Money, culture, and daily struggles often make healthy choices tough to practice.

question: Which nursing diagnosis focuses directly on blood supply to the brain tissue?

options.A: Risk for Impaired Skin Integrity
options.B: Ineffective Tissue Perfusion (Cerebral)
options.C: Impaired Physical Mobility
options.D: Ineffective Airway Clearance

explanation: You've got this! This diagnosis simply points to situations where blood and oxygen aren't reaching brain cells properly because of swelling, clots, or bleeding.

question: What makes an intraarterial line different from a standard intravenous (IV) line?

options.A: Medication is delivered directly into an artery
options.B: Infusions are always powered by gravity alone
options.C: Drugs are absorbed slowly through the digestive tract
options.D: Catheters are exclusively placed in the jugular vein

explanation: You've got this! The key difference is right in the name: instead of going into a vein like a normal IV, the catheter goes straight into an arterial blood vessel.

question: What is a major benefit of regular physical activity for older adults?

options.A: Elimination of the need for daily sleep
options.B: Complete reversal of all age-related wrinkles
options.C: Immediate restoration of lost hearing ability
options.D: Improved balance, muscle strength, and mood

explanation: Movement is medicine! Even light, tailored exercise helps seniors stay strong, lowers their risk of falls, and keeps their spirits high.

question: Why is an MRI scan so helpful when evaluating a patient with suspected CJD?

options.A: It checks the electrical activity of skeletal muscles.
options.B: It reveals characteristic patterns of brain tissue damage.
options.C: It measures the exact level of circulating antibodies.
options.D: It clears away abnormal prion protein deposits safely.

explanation: Spot on! An MRI can show distinct bright spots and damage patterns in specific areas of the brain, guiding the medical team.

question: What is the main goal of adolescent-friendly health services?

options.A: To provide welcoming healthcare that young people can access without fear or judgment
options.B: To offer free medications exclusively to children under twelve years old
options.C: To completely replace adult hospital wards with youth-only medical centers
options.D: To let teenagers prescribe their own basic treatments during clinic visits

explanation: Adolescent-friendly services are specifically designed to make young people feel safe, respected, and comfortable when seeking medical attention. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T4#GNS312_U4_T4_h1)

question: Which of these is NOT a common risk factor for stress urinary incontinence?

options.A: Obesity and excess body weight
options.B: Menopause and decreased estrogen levels
options.C: Frequent high-fluid intake throughout the day
options.D: Vaginal childbirth and multiple pregnancies

explanation: Drinking plenty of water is healthy! The real risk factors involve things that weaken pelvic support, like childbirth, hormonal shifts, or heavy pressure.

question: Which of these is a classic sign of mastitis in a breastfeeding mother?

options.A: Foul-smelling brownish lochia
options.B: Localized breast redness, pain, and fever
options.C: Complete absence of milk production
options.D: Painless bilateral breast enlargement

explanation: Mastitis means the breast tissue is inflamed or infected. You'll usually spot a painful, red, warm area on the breast along with fever and body aches.

question: You notice tidaling has suddenly stopped in the water seal chamber of a stable patient. What should you check first?

options.A: Check the tubing for kinks, blockages, or loops hanging too low
options.B: Call the surgeon to request immediate removal of the chest tube
options.C: Disconnect the drainage system from the wall suction source
options.D: Immediately clamp the chest tube with two heavy metal hemostats

explanation: Don't panic! When tidaling stops, it often just means something is blocking the tube, like a kink or a loop resting under the bed. Check the lines first.

question: What vital paper must always travel with a critically ill patient during a transfer?

options.A: A blank sheet of paper for the driver to take notes on
options.B: A detailed referral note outlining history, vital signs, and treatments given
options.C: The personal identity card of the attending nurse
options.D: A receipt for the purchase of hospital drugs

explanation: The receiving team needs to know what happened so far, what vital signs look like, and what drugs were given.

question: A nurse is teaching range-of-motion exercises to a patient recovering from a stroke. Which level of prevention is this?

options.A: Secondary prevention
options.B: Primary prevention
options.C: Primordial prevention
options.D: Tertiary prevention

explanation: Rehabilitation and preventing further disability from an established disease fall under tertiary prevention. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T91#GNS214_U1_T91_h3)

question: In developing areas, which social issue is most tied to high rates of teenage pregnancy?

options.A: Excessive participation in competitive sports
options.B: Poverty and lack of access to education
options.C: High rates of urban migration
options.D: Universal access to family planning clinics

explanation: Correct! Poverty and limited schooling often strip young girls of choices and keep them from knowing about or getting preventive reproductive care.

question: What is the main job of the parathyroid hormone (PTH)?

options.A: To stimulate the pancreas to release stored insulin
options.B: To store extra calcium directly inside the kidney tissues
options.C: To lower blood calcium by moving it into the bones
options.D: To raise blood calcium levels when they drop too low

explanation: When blood calcium gets dangerously low, PTH steps in to rescue it by pulling calcium out of the bones, saving it in the kidneys, and helping absorb more from food.

question: Why is taking a quiet pause (silence) useful during a patient interview?

options.A: It forces the patient to answer closed-ended questions
options.B: It gives the patient time to gather thoughts and reflect
options.C: It shows the nurse has lost interest in the conversation
options.D: It prevents the patient from asking difficult questions

explanation: Well done! Brief moments of silence give patients space to breathe, collect their thoughts, and share what is really on their mind.

question: What is the medical term for painful sexual intercourse experienced by many FGM survivors?

options.A: Dysphasia
options.B: Dysuria
options.C: Dyspareunia
options.D: Dysmenorrhea

explanation: Dyspareunia refers to painful intercourse, commonly caused in FGM survivors by tight scar tissue and nerve damage. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T6#GNS312_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is the main danger when a patient stops taking her antibiotics halfway just because she feels better?

options.A: Surviving germs can multiply and cause drug resistance
options.B: The laboratory will lose the record of her initial test
options.C: The patient will instantly develop a severe viral illness
options.D: Her body will stop producing any natural red blood cells

explanation: Stopping early kills off the weak germs but leaves the strongest ones alive to bounce back stronger and harder to treat!

question: What does patient confidentiality require of you as a nurse?

options.A: To refuse documentation in the official hospital medical record
options.B: To share patient secrets with any interested family member
options.C: To keep patient diagnoses hidden permanently from the care team
options.D: To protect patient health information from unauthorized disclosure

explanation: Correct! Confidentiality means keeping private health info safe and only sharing it with the healthcare team taking care of them.

question: During an IV insertion, what lets you know for sure that your needle has successfully entered the vein?

options.A: The infusion bag begins to drip rapidly without any pressure.
options.B: The surrounding skin turns pale and cool to the touch.
options.C: The patient reports a sudden cooling sensation in the arm.
options.D: A flash of blood appears inside the flashback chamber of the device.

explanation: That's right! Seeing that little 'flash' of dark red blood in the chamber is the classic sign that you're in the vein. Beautiful work!

question: Which vitamin shortage is directly linked to poor blood clotting in long-term malabsorption?

options.A: Vitamin B1
options.B: Vitamin C
options.C: Vitamin A
options.D: Vitamin K

explanation: Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin needed by the liver to make clotting factors. If fats aren't being absorbed, Vitamin K isn't either!

question: Why are sudden weight fluctuations particularly dangerous for a patient with heart failure?

options.A: They signal dangerous fluid retention
options.B: They mean the patient is eating too much salt
options.C: They indicate rapid muscle wasting
options.D: They show an immediate loss of bone mass

explanation: In heart failure, rapid weight gain almost always means the body is holding onto extra fluid that the heart cannot pump out. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T8#GNS225_U2_T8_h1)

question: What is a very common emotional experience for patients facing the end of their lives?

options.A: Existential distress and questioning life meaning
options.B: An intense desire to run marathons
options.C: Complete indifference to surroundings and people
options.D: Sudden loss of all emotional feelings

explanation: You got it! Toward the end of life, it's completely normal for patients to look back, wonder about their life's purpose, and work through big deep questions.

question: What makes hot and cold packs such great choices in everyday nursing care?

options.A: They prevent all forms of skin breakdown automatically
options.B: They completely eliminate the need for physician supervision
options.C: They work instantly to heal surgical incisions overnight
options.D: They offer a cost-effective way to help manage pain without medication

explanation: Exactly! They are affordable, readily available, and give patients that extra touch of relief alongside their regular medications.

question: Why must an antiseptic skin prep air-dry completely before inserting an IV catheter?

options.A: To allow the chemical time to kill microorganisms effectively
options.B: To ensure the vein stays dilated and easy to see
options.C: To prevent the sticky dressing from sliding off wet skin
options.D: To keep the patient from feeling a burning sensation

explanation: Antiseptics like chlorhexidine require contact time and drying to achieve their full germ-killing effect. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h5)

question: Which personal protective equipment is essential when caring for a patient with airborne tuberculosis?

options.A: An N95 respirator mask
options.B: A heavy plastic body apron
options.C: Sterile rubber cleaning boots
options.D: A standard cloth face mask

explanation: Tuberculosis travels on tiny airborne nuclei that require tight-fitting respirator filters to prevent inhalation by health workers. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T7#GNS313_U2_T7_h4)

question: Why are waste handlers considered a high-risk group for unsafe injection practices?

options.A: They frequently handle poorly disposed sharp medical waste
options.B: They process expired oral medications in the pharmacy
options.C: They administer injections to community members at home
options.D: They clean hospital floors without wearing heavy boots

explanation: Waste handlers often encounter stray needles thrown into regular trash instead of puncture-proof safety boxes. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T5#GNS122_U3_T5_h4)

question: What is an example of 'therapeutic presence' when caring for a grieving patient?

options.A: Leaving the room immediately so they can cry alone
options.B: Explaining all the scientific stages of grief to them
options.C: Sitting quietly and allowing the patient space to cry
options.D: Distracting them quickly with jokes to cheer them up

explanation: Brilliant! Sometimes the best nursing care doesn't involve words at all—just sitting quietly and showing you care is powerful.

question: What tells you that an infant is ready to come out of Gallows traction?

options.A: The baby turns two years old
options.B: The ropes are starting to look worn out
options.C: X-rays show the bone has healed well with good callus formation
options.D: The parents ask for the metal frame to be taken down

explanation: We don't guess—we check! Only an X-ray proving the bone is strong enough will greenlight removing the traction.

question: How have many religious views on family planning changed over time?

options.A: Moving toward an emphasis on responsible parenthood and maternal health
options.B: Eliminating the discussion of reproductive health in communities
options.C: Banning all forms of medical care for pregnant women
options.D: Mandating artificial contraception for all married couples

explanation: Many religious groups now embrace family planning when it's used to protect the mother's health and care responsibly for children.

question: If a needle is missing after a big surgery, what is the next step the team should take?

options.A: Ignore the discrepancy if the patient looks stable
options.B: Assume the needle evaporated and finish stitching the skin
options.C: Ask the patient to pay for a replacement needle
options.D: Perform a thorough search of the room and take an X-ray

explanation: Spot on! A missing needle means a full search of the room and an X-ray to confirm where it went. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T8#GNS123_U5_T8_h5)

question: Which fasting blood sugar level is usually the cutoff for diagnosing diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Less than 70 mg/dL
options.B: 100 to 110 mg/dL
options.C: 80 to 90 mg/dL
options.D: 126 mg/dL or higher

explanation: Keep this number handy for your clinical postings: 126 mg/dL or higher on two separate tests points toward a diabetes diagnosis.

question: What is the main goal of post-abortion care (PAC) counselling?

options.A: To punish clients who break hospital rules
options.B: To force clients to speak with law enforcement
options.C: To support clients physically and emotionally
options.D: To convince clients to change their religious beliefs

explanation: PAC counselling is all about giving compassionate physical and emotional support to help your client heal safely. As a nurse, creating a safe space makes all the difference! [learn more](GNS226_U5_T007#GNS226_U5_T007_h1)

question: When making the initial cut to drain an abscess, which direction should the surgical blade follow?

options.A: Directly perpendicular to muscle fibers
options.B: In a randomized zigzag pattern
options.C: Along the natural skin tension lines
options.D: In a wide circular shape around the border

explanation: Cutting along the body's natural skin lines (Langer's lines) helps the wound heal better and keeps scarring to a minimum.

question: Which breath test checks for problems absorbing carbs or too much bacteria in the gut?

options.A: Pulmonary function test
options.B: Arterial blood gas test
options.C: Hydrogen breath test
options.D: Sputum culture test

explanation: A hydrogen breath test measures exhaled breath after drinking certain sugars to see how well the gut is handling them.

question: Which vital sign check needs immediate nursing action after a patient takes a sedative?

options.A: Respiratory rate dropping below twelve breaths per minute
options.B: Oral temperature measuring 37 degrees Celsius
options.C: Heart rate staying steady at seventy-two beats per minute
options.D: Blood pressure reading of 120 over 80 millimeters of mercury

explanation: A slow breathing rate is a major red flag for dangerous central nervous system depression. Always watch the airway first! [learn more](GNS223_U6_T2#GNS223_U6_T2_h7)

question: In what pattern should you clean an injection site with an alcohol swab?

options.A: Up and down in long vertical strokes only
options.B: In a circular motion from the center moving outward
options.C: From the outer edges inward toward the exact center
options.D: In a harsh side-to-side scrubbing motion across the skin

explanation: Cleaning from the center outward pushes dirt and bacteria away from the spot where the needle will enter the skin. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T67#GNS214_U1_T67_h4)

question: What is the main goal that drives private companies in the food supply business?

options.A: Providing completely free meals to every global citizen
options.B: Financial profit and commercial return on investment
options.C: Enforcing international public health laws and safety codes
options.D: Eliminating the need for government agricultural policies

explanation: Private agribusinesses and food corporations are businesses, so their main engine is making a profit from what they sell.

question: What is the single best way to stop infections from spreading in any healthcare setting?

options.A: Wearing sterile gowns for every procedure
options.B: Performing proper hand hygiene
options.C: Administering prophylactic antibiotics
options.D: Using disposable plastic trays

explanation: Simple handwashing or alcohol rubbing is your superpower against hospital infections. It removes germs picked up from patients and surroundings instantly.

question: What is a major danger if a patient suddenly stops taking their long-term degenerative medications without talking to a doctor?

options.A: A sudden, severe return of symptoms or withdrawal
options.B: An immediate boost in liver and kidney function
options.C: Complete regeneration of normal nerve cells
options.D: An instant and permanent cure of the disease

explanation: You got it! Stopping chronic meds cold turkey can send the body into a severe rebound, making symptoms much worse than they were before. Tapering is usually needed!

question: What is the main reason doctors taper corticosteroid therapy down gradually instead of stopping it overnight?

options.A: To prevent the development of severe allergic skin rashes
options.B: To keep blood sugar levels artificially low during withdrawal
options.C: To allow the adrenal glands time to resume natural cortisol production
options.D: To ensure the original disease symptoms never return again

explanation: A slow taper gives the sleeping adrenal glands a gentle wakeup call so they can remember how to make their own cortisol again safely.

question: Why is deliberate silence often an effective nursing tool during end-of-life conversations?

options.A: It signals to the family that the conversation has ended
options.B: It gives the patient time to process heavy thoughts and emotions
options.C: It allows the nurse to document notes without interruption
options.D: It forces the patient to speak when they are feeling shy

explanation: End-of-life topics are emotionally heavy, and quiet moments allow patients the necessary time to gather their thoughts and speak when ready. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T6#GNS321_U4_T6_h1)

question: Which special cell type must be present to diagnose Hodgkin Lymphoma?

options.A: Epithelial cells
options.B: Reed-Sternberg cells
options.C: Plasma cells
options.D: Kupffer cells

explanation: Spotting giant, unusual Reed-Sternberg cells under a microscope is the classic giveaway that tells doctors it's Hodgkin Lymphoma!

question: What is the difference between withholding and withdrawing medical treatment?

options.A: Withholding is illegal, while withdrawing is legally permitted
options.B: There is no difference in definition, only in the cost of medications
options.C: Withholding requires court approval, while withdrawing requires only family consent
options.D: Withholding means never starting an intervention, while withdrawing means stopping an ongoing one

explanation: It's all about timing! Withholding means you decide not to start a treatment in the first place, while withdrawing means you turn off or stop a treatment that was already running.

question: What is the main biological goal of puberty during adolescence?

options.A: Completion of prefrontal cortex myelination
options.B: Rapid increase in bone mineral density only
options.C: Attaining sexual maturity and reproductive capacity
options.D: Stabilization of adult personality traits

explanation: You got this! Puberty is simply the body's natural transition to reach sexual maturity and the ability to reproduce.

question: Why do many young females struggle to insist on barrier protection like condoms during sex?

options.A: A lack of physical strength to hold the protective devices
options.B: Medical regulations prohibiting females from purchasing supplies
options.C: Power imbalances and fear of financial or physical retribution
options.D: Biological immunity that makes protection completely unnecessary

explanation: Exactly. When a partner holds all the power—or threatens violence—safe sex negotiation becomes terrifyingly difficult.

question: Which simple tool do nurses commonly use to screen adult patients for distant vision problems?

options.A: Otoscope
options.B: Snellen chart
options.C: Ophthalmoscope
options.D: Tuning fork

explanation: The Snellen chart is the classic eye chart with rows of letters that we use to check how clearly someone can see from a distance. Great clinical tool to keep in mind!

question: What is the absolute number one priority when managing a patient with a suspected drug overdose?

options.A: Securing the airway and ensuring breathing
options.B: Administering a laxative to clear the bowels
options.C: Finding out the exact name of the drug taken
options.D: Filling out the hospital admission forms

explanation: Remember your ABCs! In any emergency, stabilizing the airway, breathing, and circulation always comes before playing detective to find out what happened.

question: Which set of vital signs makes up the famous 'Cushing triad', warning us of severe brainstem compression?

options.A: Normal blood pressure, irregular pulse, and clear breath sounds
options.B: High fever, fast heart rate, and deep rapid respirations
options.C: Widening pulse pressure, slow heart rate, and irregular breathing
options.D: Low blood pressure, rapid pulse, and shallow breathing

explanation: You're doing great! The Cushing triad is a critical late warning sign. Watch out for a wide gap between top and bottom blood pressure numbers, a slow heart rate (bradycardia), and irregular breathing. It means the brainstem is in trouble!

question: When exercising the lower limbs, where should you place your hands to support the leg?

options.A: Under the knee and under the heel
options.B: Right on the kneecap and toes
options.C: Around the middle of the thigh bone
options.D: Firmly on the client's hip bones

explanation: Spot on! Supporting the leg at the knee and heel keeps the patient comfortable and gives you steady control.

question: What visual sign confirms that an intradermal injection was successfully placed in the dermis?

options.A: A small bleb or blister forms on the skin surface.
options.B: The surrounding skin turns pale and cold to the touch.
options.C: A drop of blood appears at the injection site immediately.
options.D: The medication leaks back out through the needle track.

explanation: The formation of a raised bleb proves the fluid is trapped within the tight dermal skin layers. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T6#GNS122_U1_T6_h4)

question: What are the elevated ridges on the surface of the cerebrum called?

options.A: Sulci
options.B: Ventricles
options.C: Fissures
options.D: Gyri

explanation: Gyri are the raised folds or ridges of brain tissue, while sulci are the shallow grooves between them. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T7#GNS211_U3_T7_h2)

question: Which cells swallow trapped fats inside artery walls to help form fatty streaks?

options.A: Platelets
options.B: Macrophages
options.C: Fibroblasts
options.D: Red blood cells

explanation: Macrophages are our immune cleanup cells, but when they eat too much trapped fat in the arteries, they turn into foam cells and start plaque buildup.

question: Which of these best describes a quality improvement framework in action?

options.A: Punishing staff members immediately whenever a patient complains about waiting times
options.B: Collecting clinic data to identify service gaps and testing small changes to fix them
options.C: Hiding poor treatment outcomes from hospital management to avoid criticism
options.D: Stopping all routine data collection until the end of the calendar year

explanation: You got it! Quality improvement is all about looking at data, spotting problems, and testing little tweaks to see what makes patient care better. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T2#GNS312_U5_T2_h7)

question: What is the main difference between a keloid scar and a normal hypertrophic scar?

options.A: Hypertrophic scars only happen after burns, while keloids happen after minor cuts
options.B: Keloids have weak collagen while hypertrophic scars have none
options.C: Keloids grow past the original edges of the wound, whereas hypertrophic scars do not
options.D: Hypertrophic scars shrink on their own, but keloids stay forever

explanation: The giveaway for a keloid is its stubborn tendency to keep growing outward, marching past the boundaries of the original injury, unlike a hypertrophic scar which stays within bounds.

question: When a client wants to switch to a different birth control method during a follow-up visit, what is your main job as a nurse?

options.A: Charge an extra administrative fee for changing the care plan
options.B: Refuse service until a senior medical officer approves the change
options.C: Force the client to continue the original method for at least one more year
options.D: Ensure there is no gap in contraceptive coverage to prevent unintended pregnancy

explanation: When changing methods, timing is everything. We must make sure there is no unprotected gap where an unintended pregnancy could happen.

question: What is the most crucial assessment for a nurse to do regularly on a limb with a tumor or post-op reconstruction?

options.A: Checking the patient's visual acuity and pupillary light reflex
options.B: Measuring the circumference of the chest wall every hour
options.C: Neurovascular checks for pulse, color, movement, and sensation
options.D: Auscultating bowel sounds in all four abdominal quadrants

explanation: Swelling or tumor growth can squeeze blood vessels and nerves. Regular checks help us catch circulation issues early and protect the limb!

question: What is the name of the vulnerable zone where columnar and squamous epithelium meet on the cervix?

options.A: Peritoneal cavity
options.B: Transformation zone
options.C: Vaginal fornix
options.D: Endometrial cavity

explanation: The transformation zone is the specific anatomical junction where different types of cervical cells meet, making it highly susceptible to infections and inflammation. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T14#GNS216_U5_T14_h3)

question: Why does carbon dioxide build up in the blood during hypercapnic respiratory failure?

options.A: Sudden loss of red blood cells in circulation
options.B: Primary infection of the heart valves
options.C: Inability to eliminate carbon dioxide effectively
options.D: Excessive oxygen levels in the room air

explanation: Hypercapnic just means too much CO2! When the lungs or breathing muscles are too tired to blow off carbon dioxide properly, it starts backing up in the blood.

question: A patient's lab report comes back with a critical panic value. What is your immediate nursing action?

options.A: Document the laboratory value in the chart and resume other tasks
options.B: Wait until the end of the shift to report the result during handoff
options.C: Notify the provider urgently and assess the patient at the bedside
options.D: Repeat the exact same blood draw yourself to confirm the mistake

explanation: A critical panic value means danger! Your first steps are to check on your patient right away at the bedside and notify the doctor immediately.

question: What is the main goal of scheduling rest periods for a patient with cancer-related fatigue?

options.A: Stimulating the appetite center in the brain
options.B: Preventing blood clots in the legs
options.C: Helping the patient conserve energy while staying gently active
options.D: Shrinking peripheral lymph node masses

explanation: It's all about balance! Alternating rest with light activity helps patients manage their energy without losing all their muscle strength.

question: Which specific nerve fibers in the skin are responsible for sending itch signals to the brain?

options.A: Pacinian touch receptors
options.B: Unmyelinated C-fibers
options.C: Meissner corpuscle endings
options.D: Large myelinated A-alpha fibers

explanation: Unmyelinated C-fibers are specialized nerve endings in our skin that pick up itch (pruritic) signals and carry them to the spinal cord.

question: A patient recovering from an intentional overdose is now awake and stable. What nursing action is most important?

options.A: Restricting all family visits to punish the patient for the suicide attempt
options.B: Providing continuous observation and psychological support while keeping the environment safe
options.C: Avoiding any conversation about the incident to prevent embarrassment
options.D: Discharging the patient immediately with a prescription for sedatives

explanation: You've got this. Emotional support and a safe, watch-careful environment are vital for anyone recovering from self-harm.

question: Which two blood tests do doctors frequently order to check for general inflammation in the body?

options.A: Sodium and potassium
options.B: Hemoglobin and hematocrit
options.C: ESR and CRP
options.D: BUN and creatinine

explanation: ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate) and CRP (C-Reactive Protein) are your go-to blood markers for spotting inflammation anywhere in the body.

question: When amino acids are broken down, they produce toxic ammonia. How does the body safely get rid of it?

options.A: The bone marrow stores it permanently as a solid mineral crystal
options.B: The lungs exhale it immediately as a dry nitrogen gas vapor
options.C: The liver converts it into urea for safe removal by the kidneys
options.D: The stomach uses it directly to neutralize strong gastric acids

explanation: Ammonia is dangerous to our cells, so the liver quickly changes it into a much safer substance called urea. The kidneys then filter this urea out through urine.

question: A patient has an infected wound on their right hand and notices tender lumps in their right armpit. What does this mean?

options.A: The patient has a primary blood disorder originating in the spleen
options.B: The patient is experiencing normal side effects of red blood cell breakdown
options.C: Bacteria from the hand wound are traveling through lymph vessels to the axillary nodes
options.D: Blockage of the thoracic duct has caused fluid backup in the upper extremity

explanation: Lymph drains from specific regions of the body to nearby nodes. An infection in the hand travels up the arm vessels, causing the armpit (axillary) nodes to trap the germs and swell up.

question: A patient has a stubborn rash that won't go away with standard treatment, so a skin biopsy is ordered. What is the goal?

options.A: Confirm a definitive diagnosis and guide treatment
options.B: Decontaminate the skin surface from bacterial flora
options.C: Remove all inflamed nerve endings causing itching
options.D: Prevent the rash from spreading to other body parts

explanation: When standard creams don't work, a biopsy helps pin down the exact problem so the healthcare team can choose the right medicine that actually works.

question: A patient has a blockage right at the entrance of the pulmonary trunk. Which chamber of the heart will struggle to empty its blood first?

options.A: Right atrium
options.B: Left ventricle
options.C: Right ventricle
options.D: Left atrium

explanation: The right ventricle pumps directly into the pulmonary trunk, so a blockage there creates backpressure and makes it hard for the right ventricle to empty. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T9#GNS111_U2_T9_h3)

question: What blood product is typically given to replace lost oxygen-carrying capacity in a massive haemorrhage?

options.A: Normal saline solution
options.B: Albumin protein liquid
options.C: Pure platelet concentrate
options.D: Packed red blood cells

explanation: Packed red blood cells specifically restore the hemoglobin and red blood cells needed to carry oxygen to tissues. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T4#GNS123_U3_T4_h7)

question: How often should a client receive a DMPA (Depo-Provera) injection for birth control?

options.A: Every 6 months
options.B: Every 1 month
options.C: Every 3 months
options.D: Every 2 months

explanation: You've got this! DMPA gives steady hormonal protection when given once every 3 months (about 13 weeks).

question: What nursing term is used to document painful menstrual cramps?

options.A: Amenorrhea
options.B: Dysmenorrhea
options.C: Metrorrhagia
options.D: Menorrhagia

explanation: Dysmenorrhea is just the professional word for painful periods. 'Dys' means painful or difficult, and 'menorrhea' refers to menstruation!

question: Which process causes the liver to release stored sugar into the blood when the body is low on insulin?

options.A: Glycolysis
options.B: Lipogenesis
options.C: Glycogenolysis
options.D: Erythropoiesis

explanation: Glycogenolysis is just a fancy medical word for breaking down stored sugar (glycogen) into glucose so the body can use it when energy is running low. You've got this!

question: Why do we make sure hospital beds are free of wrinkles and crumbs?

options.A: To reduce the physical weight of the mattress during turns
options.B: To prevent skin irritation and pressure sores
options.C: To make it easier to transfer patients to a wheelchair
options.D: To comply with dietary and housekeeping rules

explanation: Great job! Tiny crumbs and creases put constant pressure on fragile patient skin, which quickly turns into painful bedsores. Keeping the bed smooth is a vital part of nursing care!

question: How do migrating cancer cells manage to break into nearby blood vessels?

options.A: They secrete enzymes that break down surrounding tissue barriers
options.B: They attract white blood cells to carry them into circulation
options.C: They wait for the blood vessel walls to rupture from high pressure
options.D: They shrink in size until they slip through normal cell walls

explanation: Spot on! Cancer cells release special chemical enzymes that chew through tissue barriers and blood vessel walls, letting them slip right into circulation.

question: Which laboratory test is used to definitively diagnose sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
options.B: Coagulation profile test
options.C: Complete blood count
options.D: Haemoglobin electrophoresis

explanation: Haemoglobin electrophoresis is the gold standard test! It separates different types of haemoglobin in a sample so the lab can clearly spot abnormal haemoglobin S.

question: A patient taking five different medications at different times of the day is most likely to experience non-compliance due to...

options.A: complete absence of any possible side effects
options.B: excessive financial savings from bulk buying
options.C: immediate physical healing from all conditions
options.D: a confusing and overwhelming pill schedule

explanation: Complex drug regimens with multiple timings cause heavy fatigue and confusion, making it very easy to miss doses. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T5#GNS215_U4_T5_h2)

question: What does a holistic approach mean in palliative care?

options.A: Addressing physical, emotional, and spiritual needs together
options.B: Focusing exclusively on spiritual counseling
options.C: Relying entirely on herbal remedies and local roots
options.D: Treating only the physical pain of the patient

explanation: A holistic approach looks at the *whole* person—body, mind, and spirit. We don't just treat a sore body; we care for the heart and mind too!

question: Why are women more likely to get bladder infections than men?

options.A: The female bladder lacks any form of transitional epithelial lining
options.B: Women produce significantly less urine volume over a 24-hour period
options.C: The female urethra is much shorter and closer to the anal opening
options.D: The female trigone is larger and traps bacteria much more easily

explanation: Anatomy plays a big role here! The female urethra is only about four centimeters long, giving outside bacteria a short and easy path straight into the bladder.

question: Which skin change is a classic sign of chronic primary adrenal insufficiency, also known as Addison's disease?

options.A: Flushing
options.B: Hyperpigmentation
options.C: Jaundice
options.D: Cyanosis

explanation: In Addison's disease, low cortisol makes the brain pump out extra ACTH, which accidentally darkens the skin, especially over knuckles and pressure points. It's a classic clinical clue!

question: Why do patients still need supportive care (like IV fluids and oxygen) even after getting an antidote?

options.A: Antidotes usually worsen the patient's baseline vital signs
options.B: Supportive care keeps the patient stable while the body handles the toxin
options.C: Supportive care replaces the need for any toxicological screening
options.D: Antidotes are completely ineffective without continuous intravenous fluids

explanation: Antidotes are amazing, but they aren't instant magic. Supportive care keeps the patient breathing and stable while the antidote and the body do the heavy lifting to clear the poison.

question: What is the main goal of the intensive phase of TB treatment?

options.A: To test if the patient is allergic to all four drugs
options.B: To rapidly reduce the bacterial load and stop infectiousness
options.C: To rebuild the damaged lung tissue back to normal
options.D: To completely finish the entire course of treatment

explanation: Hitting TB hard with four drugs quickly drops the germ count so the patient stops spreading it to others. Excellent clinical milestone!

question: Which physical examination technique is rarely used today for routine heart checks?

options.A: Auscultation
options.B: Inspection
options.C: Percussion
options.D: Palpation

explanation: Percussion has been largely replaced by modern imaging like X-rays and echocardiograms because those methods provide much clearer results. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T2#GNS213_U1_T2_h3)

question: Why does severe facial and body swelling occur in nephrotic syndrome?

options.A: Low blood protein reduces pressure that keeps fluid inside blood vessels
options.B: Infections block the lymphatic system in the neck and face
options.C: The heart pumps too much blood for the kidneys to handle
options.D: Excess salt intake causes the body to sweat less

explanation: When albumin levels drop in the blood, the pulling pressure that keeps water inside the blood vessels is lost, causing fluid to leak into tissues. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T8#GNS213_U4_T8_h1)

question: What health education should a nurse give a patient taking antibiotics for a bite wound?

options.A: Stop taking the medication as soon as the pain disappears
options.B: Double the dose if redness starts to spread around the edges
options.C: Crush the pills and mix them directly into the open wound
options.D: Finish every single pill, even if the wound looks completely healed

explanation: Always remind patients to complete their full antibiotic course so the infection is wiped out completely and resistance doesn't develop.

question: A pregnant teenager at her antenatal visit says her family expects a local nurse to circumcise her newborn daughter. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Send the family to a traditional cutter who uses sterile tools
options.B: Offer to do it quietly at the clinic to avoid infections
options.C: Ignore it since cultural practices are none of a nurse's business
options.D: Educate the mother firmly on the severe health risks and legal penalties of FGM

explanation: Spot on! Nurses must actively educate patients against FGM, uphold professional ethics, and make it clear that medicalized cutting is both illegal and unethical.

question: What is an easy, key nursing action to help prevent pneumonia in patients on a breathing machine (ventilator)?

options.A: Changing the endotracheal tube every twelve hours
options.B: Administering intravenous antibiotics to all ventilated patients
options.C: Keeping the room temperature below twenty degrees Celsius
options.D: Elevating the head of the bed between 30 and 45 degrees

explanation: Raising the bed head keeps oral and stomach secretions from sliding down into the lungs. Simple position changes make a massive difference!

question: What is the main way targeted cancer therapy drugs fight the disease?

options.A: They physically trap circulating tumor cells inside the liver.
options.B: They emit local ionizing radiation directly inside the blood vessels.
options.C: They replace the patient's damaged bone marrow with healthy donor cells.
options.D: They block specific molecules and growth pathways unique to cancer cells.

explanation: Brilliant! Unlike regular chemo, targeted therapy acts like a smart missile, zeroing in on specific chemical signals that tumors use to grow.

question: What routine self-care practice is strongly emphasized to patients at risk for infective endocarditis to prevent bacteria from entering the bloodstream?

options.A: Refusing all routine vaccinations at local health clinics
options.B: Drinking large quantities of palm wine daily
options.C: Maintaining good oral hygiene and regular dental check-ups
options.D: Avoiding all physical exercise for the rest of their lives

explanation: Oral bacteria can easily enter the bloodstream during dental procedures or daily hygiene, making dental care a primary prevention target for endocarditis. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T7#GNS213_U1_T7_h8)

question: What is the primary rule when examining a limb for musculoskeletal problems?

options.A: Always use a goniometer during the initial inspection phase
options.B: Always examine the lower extremities before the upper extremities
options.C: Always start by performing an X-ray before touching the limb
options.D: Always compare the affected side with the unaffected side

explanation: Comparing the injured or painful limb to the healthy side gives the nurse a baseline of what is normal for that specific patient. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T3#GNS222_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why do nurses need to look beyond the hospital walls when caring for patients?

options.A: Clinical treatments alone are completely useless without government approval
options.B: Patients expect nurses to solve their personal family conflicts
options.C: Hospital regulations require documentation of a patient's financial status
options.D: External economic, social, and cultural forces deeply shape a person's health outcomes

explanation: You've got this! Remember that health doesn't start and stop at the hospital doors. A patient's daily life, money, and community heavily influence their healing. [learn more](GNS216_U1_T6#GNS216_U1_T6_h1)

question: At what cervical dilation does the active phase of normal labor officially start on a partograph?

options.A: 8 centimeters
options.B: 10 centimeters
options.C: 1 centimeter
options.D: 4 centimeters

explanation: 4 centimeters is your magic marker! That is where the active phase of labor officially begins on the partograph.

question: Why should nurses avoid routine, scheduled suctioning of a breathing tube when the patient doesn't actually need it?

options.A: It increases the risk of accidental tube decannulation
options.B: It automatically changes the prescribed ventilator tidal volume
options.C: It can cause mucosal trauma, bleeding, and low oxygen levels
options.D: It causes the ventilator to trigger persistent low-pressure alarms

explanation: Suctioning is helpful when there's mucus, but doing it too often irritates the airway lining and robs the lungs of precious oxygen. Only suction when necessary!

question: How can a nurse manager best handle frequent equipment shortages during daily ward activities?

options.A: Refuse to admit any new patients until funding improves
options.B: Blame the junior nurses for failing to improvise supplies
options.C: Ignore the missing equipment and ask patients to buy everything
options.D: Maximise available resources and advocate for better supply systems

explanation: You're thinking like a true leader! A great manager makes the best of what's on hand while constantly pushing upper management for better supplies.

question: Why is it important for nurses to get involved in community advocacy and health policies, alongside bedside care?

options.A: Adolescents never listen to advice given inside a hospital consultation room
options.B: Policy enforcement is the only task that generates revenue for health centers
options.C: Environmental and structural dangers cannot be fixed solely by treating individuals
options.D: Hospitals forbid nurses from performing any clinical procedures without laws

explanation: Brilliant! Treating injuries at the bedside is only half the battle. Community and policy changes are needed to tackle the root causes of danger in society.

question: What is the primary focus of Primary Health Care compared to tertiary hospital care?

options.A: Community-level prevention and basic health promotion
options.B: Providing exclusive care for wealthy urban citizens
options.C: Advanced surgical procedures and organ transplants
options.D: Managing rare and complicated genetic diseases

explanation: Primary Health Care brings essential, everyday health services and disease prevention directly into local communities. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T4#GNS124_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which of these is a common physical sign of normal grief?

options.A: Total permanent loss of appetite and thirst
options.B: Tightness in the chest and heavy fatigue
options.C: Severe visual and auditory hallucinations
options.D: Fixed neurological paralysis of the limbs

explanation: Great job! Grief isn't just emotional; it takes a physical toll on the body, often causing heavy tiredness and chest tightness.

question: How is the malaria parasite (Plasmodium) most commonly spread in Nigeria?

options.A: Inhalation of airborne droplets
options.B: Bite of the female Anopheles mosquito
options.C: Ingestion of poorly washed vegetables
options.D: Direct person-to-person skin contact

explanation: You've got this! Infected female Anopheles mosquitoes carry the malaria parasite and pass it into the bloodstream when they bite.

question: How do nurses best create a supportive clinical environment for FGM survivors?

options.A: By offering empathetic listening, privacy, and non-judgmental care
options.B: By refusing to treat patients who refuse surgery
options.C: By discouraging patients from talking about their pain
options.D: By asking intrusive questions in front of waiting crowds

explanation: That's right! A warm, private, and non-judgmental approach lowers patient anxiety and encourages them to keep coming back for care. [learn more](GNS312_U1_T8#GNS312_U1_T8_h7)

question: Why is having a nurse stay close and encourage a mother during active labor so helpful?

options.A: it directly accelerates cervical effacement by stimulating oxytocin receptors
options.B: it completely eliminates the biological need for pharmacological anesthesia
options.C: it helps reduce maternal anxiety and decreases the perceived intensity of pain
options.D: it prevents the occurrence of variable decelerations in the fetal heart rate

explanation: Well done! Continuous presence and a warm, reassuring voice lower stress and help mothers cope much better with contractions.

question: What metabolic issue is closely linked to high male hormone levels in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?

options.A: Insulin resistance
options.B: Iron deficiency
options.C: Taking too much Vitamin C
options.D: Eating too much salt

explanation: Spot on! When the body shows insulin resistance, insulin levels rise, which triggers the ovaries to pump out extra androgens.

question: Which of these is an important warning sign you must teach a patient before they go home after a proctoscopy?

options.A: Normal resumption of eating food
options.B: Heavy or continuous rectal bleeding
options.C: Mild passing of gas for two hours
options.D: A temporary feeling of rectal fullness

explanation: Spot on! A tiny bit of spotting can happen, but heavy or ongoing bleeding is not normal. Always tell patients to report this right away.

question: A patient with end-stage kidney disease complains of severe itching all over their body. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: An allergic reaction to the standard hospital soap used during morning care
options.B: Mineral imbalances causing calcium-phosphate crystals to deposit in the skin tissues
options.C: Excessive production of red blood cells causing severe pressure under the skin
options.D: A sudden viral skin infection caused by a weakened immune system

explanation: Poor kidneys struggle to balance calcium and phosphorus. When phosphorus builds up, tiny mineral crystals form under the skin, causing that intense, frustrating itch.

question: Which of the following is an example of objective, professional nursing documentation?

options.A: Client is a difficult person who hates taking medications.
options.B: Client looks lazy and refuses to get out of bed.
options.C: Client cried during family visits and verbalized feeling hopeless.
options.D: Client is acting crazy and refusing to talk to anyone today.

explanation: Professional documentation records observable behaviors and direct client statements without personal judgment or bias. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T5#GNS222_U3_T5_h8)

question: If a patient's blood pressure drops suddenly, how does the body try to fix it right away?

options.A: Immediate reduction in breathing rate
options.B: Widespread widening of all blood vessels
options.C: A major decrease in the overall heart rate
options.D: Tightening blood vessels and speeding up the heart

explanation: To protect vital organs when pressure drops, the nervous system acts fast: it squeezes blood vessels (vasoconstriction) and makes the heart beat faster to keep blood moving!

question: How much food should you put on the spoon when feeding an adult patient?

options.A: Just a single tiny drop
options.B: One-third to one-half full
options.C: Overflowing with extra gravy
options.D: Packed tightly to the very top

explanation: Smaller spoonfuls are much easier and safer for the patient to chew and swallow without getting overwhelmed.

question: What natural biological feature in adolescent females makes them more vulnerable to certain sexually transmitted infections?

options.A: Cervical ectopy
options.B: Enlarged ovarian follicles
options.C: Thickened endometrial lining
options.D: Hyperactive uterine peristalsis

explanation: You nailed it! Cervical ectopy exposes more delicate cells on the outer cervix, making young women biologically more susceptible to infections.

question: How does activated charcoal help treat someone who swallowed a poison?

options.A: It dilates blood vessels to speed up renal excretion
options.B: It coats the lungs to block toxic gas inhalation
options.C: It binds to toxins in the gut to prevent their absorption into the bloodstream
options.D: It neutralizes stomach acid to prevent chemical ulcers

explanation: Activated charcoal acts like a microscopic sponge, holding onto the toxins in the stomach and gut so they don't enter the bloodstream.

question: What is a common physical sign that an adolescent is experiencing chronic emotional stress from unsupportive relationships?

options.A: A permanent change in natural eye color
options.B: Sudden increase in height and shoe size
options.C: Rapid healing of minor skin scratches
options.D: Frequent unexplained headaches and stomachaches

explanation: Emotional distress often shows up as physical symptoms, known as somatic complaints, when teenagers face toxic environments at home or school. [learn more](GNS312_U3_T20#GNS312_U3_T20_h3)

question: When should you seal and replace a sharps disposal box?

options.A: When it is completely filled to the absolute brim
options.B: Whenever the outer cardboard gets slightly dusty
options.C: When it is three-quarters full
options.D: At the end of every single calendar month

explanation: Stop at the three-quarter mark! Waiting until it's overflowing invites accidental needle pricks.

question: A teenage client is super shy and hesitant to talk about sexual health. What should you do first as their nurse?

options.A: Create a safe, confidential, and non-judgmental environment
options.B: Call the client's parents into the room immediately
options.C: Skip the sexual health assessment entirely
options.D: Scold the client for being immature about health matters

explanation: Brilliant nursing instinct! Trust and a warm, welcoming vibe help nervous clients relax and open up to care.

question: What makes hepatorenal syndrome different from regular kidney failure?

options.A: Kidneys stop working because of high blood sugar
options.B: It only happens to people with healthy livers
options.C: It causes permanent physical damage to kidney tissue
options.D: The kidneys fail due to altered blood flow, not physical injury

explanation: Spot on! Hepatorenal syndrome happens because of severe blood circulation changes caused by liver issues—the kidney tissue itself isn't physically damaged at first. Excellent clinical insight!

question: Why do nurses document patient care?

options.A: To prove the nurse worked a full shift
options.B: To provide data for hospital billing only
options.C: To replace verbal handovers entirely
options.D: To communicate care among the healthcare team

explanation: Great job! Writing things down ensures doctors, nurses on other shifts, and therapists all know what is happening with your patient.

question: A nurse starts a support group for people living with sickle cell across the entire state. What type of community is this?

options.A: Geopolitical community
options.B: Municipal community
options.C: Phenomenological community
options.D: Structural community

explanation: You're getting it! When people are united by a shared experience or health condition rather than just living on the same street, it's a phenomenological community.

question: Why would a doctor order an antibody blood test for someone with a suspected endocrine problem?

options.A: To test how quickly the kidneys filter out waste products
options.B: To determine if the patient has a bacterial infection
options.C: To check for autoimmune destruction of endocrine tissue
options.D: To measure the exact weight and size of the pituitary gland

explanation: Spot on! Antibody tests help us see if the body's immune system is mistakenly attacking its own hormone glands, like in thyroid disorders.

question: A patient with uncontrolled diabetes complains of a constant burning and shooting pain in their feet. What type of pain is this?

options.A: Somatic pain
options.B: Nociceptive pain
options.C: Visceral pain
options.D: Neuropathic pain

explanation: Neuropathic pain comes directly from nerve damage (like from high blood sugar over time). It often feels like burning, tingling, or shooting pain.

question: A patient having a severe asthma attack gets an intravenous steroid. What is the main goal of giving this in an emergency?

options.A: To thin out thick mucus plugs blocking the lower lung passages
options.B: To immediately relax tightened smooth muscle bands around the windpipe
options.C: To boost the patient's heart rate and increase oxygen delivery
options.D: To reduce swelling and inflammation inside the bronchial airways

explanation: Remember, steroids take a little time to change gene expression, so they aren't quick-fix muscle relaxers—they are used to bring down the dangerous swelling inside the airways.

question: A nurse wipes down a bedside table with a chemical disinfectant. What is the expected result?

options.A: Most pathogenic germs are killed, but bacterial spores may survive
options.B: The surface becomes completely sterile for surgical procedures
options.C: All living microorganisms and tough spores are completely destroyed
options.D: Only visible dust and physical dirt are physically washed away

explanation: Disinfectants are great for cleaning surfaces and killing most harmful germs, but they don't always wipe out tough bacterial spores.

question: What physical feature of capillaries makes the exchange of substances possible?

options.A: Walls that are only one cell thick
options.B: Direct connections to large veins
options.C: Valves that stop blood from flowing backward
options.D: Thick muscular layers that pulse strongly

explanation: The ultra-thin single-cell wall of a capillary allows easy diffusion of gases and nutrients between blood and tissue cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T12#GNS111_U2_T12_h4)

question: About how much total cerebrospinal fluid does the human body produce every 24 hours?

options.A: 15 milliliters
options.B: 500 milliliters
options.C: 50 milliliters
options.D: 5 liters

explanation: You got it! Our bodies continuously refresh our CSF, making about 500 milliliters every single day.

question: Why is oophoritis rarely found completely by itself in the clinic?

options.A: The ovaries have a thick capsule that blocks everything
options.B: Diagnostic ultrasound cannot see the ovaries separately
options.C: It usually spreads to the fallopian tubes and nearby pelvic organs
options.D: Ovarian swelling never happens without pregnancy

explanation: Think of the pelvic organs as close neighbors. An infection in one easily spreads to the others, which is why oophoritis usually happens alongside pelvic inflammatory disease (PID).

question: Why must nurses take a proactive approach rather than waiting for problems to fix themselves?

options.A: Doctors rarely check on patients unless a nurse calls first
options.B: Small clinical issues can rapidly turn into major emergencies
options.C: Proactive nurses are excused from doing routine bedside care
options.D: Hospital policies require nurses to document every minor event

explanation: Acting early prevents minor changes in a patient's condition from worsening into critical crises. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T7#GNS112_U3_T7_h1)

question: Why is supportive care so crucial when treating newly emerging infectious diseases?

options.A: Specific targeted medications may not yet exist for new pathogens
options.B: Patients recover much faster without receiving any fluids
options.C: Medications are forbidden in federal isolation treatment centers
options.D: Supportive care permanently changes the genetic code of a virus

explanation: Because new pathogens take time to study, treatments often rely on supporting the body's organs until the immune system fights it off. [learn more](GNS123_U4_T5#GNS123_U4_T5_h8)

question: What is the best immediate nursing action after a client finishes the final blood draw of a GTT?

options.A: Instruct the client to continue fasting until they get home
options.B: Administer a small dose of oral insulin to prevent a sugar spike
options.C: Encourage the client to exercise vigorously to burn off the sugar
options.D: Provide a snack containing protein and complex carbohydrates

explanation: Eating a balanced snack helps stabilize blood sugar and prevents the dizziness or fatigue caused by reactive hypoglycemia. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T20#GNS222_U2_T20_h7)

question: Why should a surgical knot be positioned to the side of the wound incision rather than directly over it?

options.A: To make it easier for the patient to pull out later
options.B: To prevent pressure on the wound line that can slow healing
options.C: To ensure the local anesthetic stays active longer
options.D: To save suture material during the procedure

explanation: Placing knots off-center prevents direct pressure and irritation on the healing skin edge underneath. [learn more](GNS311_U4_T3#GNS311_U4_T3_h5)

question: Why might a newly diagnosed patient temporarily use the defense mechanism of denial?

options.A: To protect the mind from overwhelming emotional pain
options.B: To increase their physical strength and immunity
options.C: To speed up cellular regeneration and wound healing
options.D: To permanently cure their underlying medical condition
